text: Per il permesso di soggiorno, cosa porti in questura?
why: 'the questura' is left in Italian in the English line, so the English doesn't translate it; an American learner doesn't know the word.
fix: For your residence permit, what do you bring to the police headquarters (questura)?

text: Glielo dico io.
why: Drops the emphasis of the stressed 'io' (I'll be the one to tell him); 'I'll tell him' loses it.
fix: I'll tell him myself.

text: Non ti preoccupare, glielo dico io.
why: Same: the stressed 'io' is the point of the reassurance and the English drops it.
fix: Don't worry, I'll tell him myself.

text: Il titolare è la persona alla quale è intestata la carta.
why: 'account holder' adds meaning; the sentence is about the card, so titolare here is the cardholder.
fix: The cardholder is the person whose name is on the card.

text: Prima di aprire il conto, mi serve il Suo codice fiscale.
why: 'tax code' is not American for a personal number; in the US 'tax code' means tax law. Americans say tax ID number.
fix: Before we open the account, I need your tax ID number.

text: Prima di aprire il conto, mi serve il codice fiscale.
why: Same 'tax code' problem.
fix: Before I open the account, I need my tax ID number.

text: Hai detto che il corso è pesante. È difficile?
why: 'heavy going' is British; an American wouldn't say it.
fix: You said the course is a grind. Is it hard?

text: È meglio che Lei non beva caffè dopo pranzo.
why: 'You'd better' is a warning in American English, stronger than the gentle advice of 'è meglio che', and loses the formal Lei register.
fix: It's best if you don't have coffee after lunch.

text: È meglio che tu non beva caffè la sera.
why: 'You'd better' sounds like a warning; è meglio che is friendly advice.
fix: It's better if you don't drink coffee in the evening.

text: È meglio che tu non beva caffè la sera.
why: Same: 'You'd better' reads as a threat or warning, not advice.
fix: It's better if you don't drink coffee in the evening.

text: Te la presto, purché tu me la riporti stasera.
why: Drops 'Te la presto' (I'll lend it to you) and adds 'Sure'; the English no longer says what the Italian says.
fix: I'll lend it to you, as long as you bring it back tonight.

text: Te la presto, purché tu me la riporti domenica.
why: Drops 'Te la presto' and replaces it with 'Sure'.
fix: I'll lend it to you, as long as you bring it back on Sunday.

text: Te la presto, purché tu me la riporti stasera.
why: Drops 'Te la presto'; the learner says a sentence the English doesn't match.
fix: I'll lend it to you, as long as you bring it back tonight.

text: Ognuno ha il suo numero: adesso tocca al quarantadue.
why: "it's forty-two's turn" is not how Americans say it; we call the number.
fix: Everyone has a number, and now it's number forty-two's turn.

text: Fa freddo e sei al bar. Cosa vuoi bere?
why: An Italian bar is a café; in American English 'the bar' means a place for alcohol, which clashes with ordering something hot.
fix: It's cold and you're at the café. What do you want to drink?

text: Gentile dottoressa Rossi,
why: 'Dr.' adds meaning: dottoressa is a courtesy title for any graduate, and an American reads Dr. as an MD or PhD. For a school office, Ms. is the equivalent.
fix: Dear Ms. Rossi,

text: Gentile dottoressa Rossi,
why: Same 'Dr.' problem.
fix: Dear Ms. Rossi,

text: Gentile dottoressa Rossi, Le scrivo per chiedere informazioni sul corso.
why: Same 'Dr.' problem.
fix: Dear Ms. Rossi, I'm writing to ask for information about the course.

text: La città: il mercante le ha lasciato tutto.
why: 'left it everything' is word-for-word and awkward English.
fix: The town. The merchant left everything to it.

text: Vuoi fotografare un affresco. Cosa chiedi al custode?
why: In American English 'custodian' means a janitor; in a church or museum the custode is the attendant or guard.
fix: You want to photograph a fresco. What do you ask the attendant?
